groups.label: Absence of Progress Idea
groups.summary: Ancient thinkers like Plato and Aristotle lacked the modern idea of progress, conceiving history instead as cyclical destructions and reconstructions governed by fate and chance.
groups.rationale: This entry stands apart as modern introductory editorial commentary analyzing ancient views on historical cycles, distinct from the dramatic dialogue of Books I through III.

groups.label: Debates on Justice in Book I
groups.summary: In Book I, Socrates and Thrasymachus contest the essence of justice and rule. Thrasymachus defines justice as the advantage of the stronger and portrays the ruler qua ruler as unerring, while Socrates counters that genuine arts serve their subjects, the just craftsman seeks no undue advantage, injustice breeds division, and justice constitutes the vital excellence of the soul.
groups.rationale: These seven contiguous entries cover the core philosophical debate in Book I between Socrates and Thrasymachus regarding justice, the role of rulers, and the soul's function.

groups.label: Nature of Goods and the State
groups.summary: Glaucon categorizes goods and presents the view of justice as a compromise arising from a social compact. In response, Socrates traces the origin of the state to human interdependence and establishes that civic efficiency relies on natural specialization and the division of labour.
groups.rationale: These Book II entries examine the baseline motivations for human association, moving from Glaucon's challenge on goods and justice to Socrates's initial construction of the city.

groups.label: Theological and Poetic Education
groups.summary: Socrates establishes theological standards that portray the divine as unchangeable and the source solely of good, while classifying the modes of poetic narration. He further prescribes an educational program where simplicity, musical harmony, and physical training jointly attune the spirited and philosophical elements of the soul.
groups.rationale: These Book II and III entries form a coherent sequence detailing the censorship of theology, forms of poetic narration, and the musical and gymnastic training of guardians.
